description: We’re LUNA (Lunar Unit for Navigation and Analysis), a team of friends who share an interest in engineering, design, and space exploration. We joined NASA Space Apps to learn together and help students understand how landing sites are chosen on the Moon.
summary: Our project is an application called LUNA, an interactive tool designed to assess the operational feasibility of different sites at the lunar south pole. Using selected strategic regions—specifically Connecting Ridge and the rim of Shackleton Crater—LUNA visualizes how the positions of the Sun and Earth change over time relative to the local terrain horizon. This makes it possible to assess how effectively each location could support solar power generation and direct communication with Earth during a space mission. Unlike traditional theoretical approaches that assume a flat surface, LUNA combines real topographic data with high-precision astronomical ephemerides. It also incorporates an interactive physical model that translates the geometric calculations into a tangible visual demonstration.
details:
LUNA is an interactive application that compares sunlight and Earth visibility conditions at two locations near the lunar south pole: Connecting Ridge and the Shackleton rim. Its purpose is to make these conditions easier to understand and support preliminary planning for future missions.

We use NASA JPL Horizons data to obtain the Sun’s and Earth’s azimuth and elevation as seen from both sites. We combine this information with NASA LRO/LOLA digital elevation models to estimate terrain obstructions in each direction. The application allows users to explore different dates, compare an ideal horizon with the local terrain horizon, and calculate joint coverage: the percentage of time when both bodies are above the selected horizon. It also evaluates operating periods of 24, 48, and 72 hours.

LUNA’s main benefit is turning complex scientific data into visual, accessible information that is easy to compare. We aim to bring lunar science closer to students, educators, and interested members of the public, demonstrating why a mission’s location and timing must be assessed together.

We developed the interface and application using Figma Make, with React, TypeScript, and CSS. We processed elevation models using Python and used TXT ephemeris files and CSV horizon profiles. We complemented the application with a 3D-printed model that demonstrates how terrain creates shadows.

The project’s creativity lies in combining synchronized comparisons over time, a 3D lunar visualization, and a physical demonstration. This allows users to observe the results and understand the phenomenon behind them.

During development, we considered site coordinates and elevations, synchronization in Universal Time, the temporal resolution of the data, and terrain obstructions. We also recognize the prototype’s limitations: horizon profiles cover only the available local terrain, and calculations based on hourly samples are approximate. Sun visibility does not guarantee sufficient power, and Earth visibility does not guarantee a radio connection. Our percentages represent joint coverage, not landing success probabilities or a complete landing safety assessment.
